title: Tau In the Clinic, Again
body_text: As readers will well know, I have been unrestrained in my opinion of the anti-amyloid antibody therapies for Alzheimer’s disease. I think that they show remarkably small levels of efficacy, quite possibly invisible to the untrained eye, at great financial cost. And what’s more, they come with significant risks of cerebral cardiovascular events, and the data are far more clear on that point than on any cognitive benefits. I think it should go without saying that if removing amyloid deposits from the brain really helped Alzheimer’s patients that you would expect much more benefit than this, because there seems little doubt that these antibodies do accomplish that. But that has meant that they are a perhaps cure for amyloid and not anything remotely approaching a cure for Alzheimer’s disease. There’s always been an interest in the deposition of tau protein in the brain, which is clearly another feature Alzheimer’s pathology. And as the evidence has piled up that amyloid by itself is not going to be the answer in this disease, tau has been on the upswing for some years. But it has to be said that the two anti-tau antibodies that have gone into the clinic have produced very disappointing results. And now we have another direct test of this idea in human patients: Diranersen, an antisense oligo from Biogen and Ionis directed against tau production itself. Phase II results on this one were reported today. . .and one gets this eeries sense of having seen this plotline before somehow. You can easily find headlines today about the drug showing progress, slowing Alzheimer’s, all the rest of it, but the real giveaway is in this Stat headline: “Biogen Alzheimer’s drug slowed decline in line with approved therapies, study shows”. In line, that is, with the two antibodies that I was just going on about, that I feel never should have been approved in the first place and that provide little of any meaningful benefit to actual Alzheimer’s patients. In line with those. Great, eh? This is done on the same cognitive-scale rating used to show the alleged benefits of those antibodies, and it’s right in the same disappointing, unimpressive range. These results (Biogen had already announced) were good enough for them to move into a larger Phase III study, and all I can do is wish them luck and be glad that I’m not invested in this program. There are a lot of oddities about the data. For example, the lower-dose patients seem to have shown greater benefit, if benefit there be, even though the higher doses seem clearly to have led to greater reductions in tau protein. Now there certainly are things such as U-shaped dose response curves, but still. As with amyloid, it seems again that it should go without saying that if tau really were as key a player in Alzheimer’s pathology as one might have hoped, that these are not the results that one would have expected. Either in direction or in magnitude. I find it hard to believe that the Phase III data are going to make a real difference in this story, and that Biogen will find itself - once again - trying to convince people that their Alzheimer’s drug candidate is a lot better than it looks, really, truly. The financial markets seem to agree: both Ionis and Biogen are down significantly today, perhaps from traders who were hyped up for something more impressive. They must not have been trading on Alzheimer’s news for very long, . .
